newsitem.title: CHINA: Metals trade asks if China can fill zinc breach.
newsitem.headline: Metals trade asks if China can fill zinc breach.

text.p: Western zinc producers and traders are questioning China's ability to crank up production of the metal to take advantage of a looming world deficit, but a major Chinese smelter said on Thursday it had no doubts.

China's Zhuzhou smelter has enough raw material on hand to boost production in the near term, and is looking to export directly to the United States where demand is firm, a marketing executive at the factory said.

"We've got 30,000 to 40,000 tonnes of concentrate stockpiled here," he said by telephone from the smelter in central Hunan province. Other sources said this was three months' supply. "We're talking to end-users in the United States about exporting direct -- that's where the demand is, not in Asia, so it makes sense," the Zhuzhou source said.

Traders and Western producers polled by Reuters wondered aloud how fast Chinese smelters could boost production to take advantage of current strong prices and a deficit in the second half of 1997 expected to be up to 270,000 tonnes.
They said zinc concentrate, the raw material of zinc metal, is in short world supply, and that demand is now focused in the United States and Europe, where China has no direct links to end users.
China produces around 1.2 million tonnes of zinc per year, and exports, on average, around 300,000 tonnes, traders said.
An Asian trader said Chinese producers this year wanted to export a total of 400,000 tonnes, adding "with this they can either go to the LME or they go to the customers".
The London Metal Exchange zinc cash price hit a 4-1/2 year high of 58.3 cents a pound on March 17, up 26 percent since December 10.
LME zinc closed on Wednesday at $1,241 per tonne, down $18.
An analyst with Macquarie Bank Group said this week additional Chinese exports in 1997, on higher prices and added capacity, would not upset the positive market outlook.
Prices would continue to trend higher, Jim Lennon said, because of the shortage of zinc concentrate production.
He put the 1997 market deficit at 270,000 tonnes and the 1998 deficit at 130,000 tonnes.
A trader in Hong Kong dismissed the notion that China is having trouble sourcing zinc concentrate.
"When the price is high, then you don't really have a problem getting the concentrate," he said, adding that China gets its concentrate from Australia.
An Australian producer source echoed market concerns that China is unable to source enough concentrate.
But the Zhuzhou marketing executive said: "China has enough." He had no figures other than for Zhuzhou.
"Taking advantage of the world price rally is a great idea, but you've got to get the raw material and put it through the system first," another producer source said.
"If people weren't producing concentrate in large amounts in 1996, it takes a while to crank up production just because the price has jumped for two months in 1997," he said.
He and others wondered how soon Chinese producers could establish direct contact with U.S. users.
"I don't think they've done it before, that's the only thing," a trader said.
"If they want to start exporting in large lumps then it's got to go to Europe and the U.S. and it hasn't really been tested that way before. It may happen."
Chinese producers generally ship their metal to LME-supervised warehouses in Singapore, where it is often used as collateral for loans.
